**Behavioral integration** — how an organism's many control systems come to act as one — action selection and competition between systems (habitual and goal-directed, automatic and willed), hierarchical and feedback control, intertemporal conflict and self-control, and evidence accumulation to a decision. One of four unities kept apart (ADR-024).

It recovers Bayes-adaptive RL in the zero-temperature limit. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md)), from the arXiv preprint, whose displayed equations did not survive text extraction. | [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) | Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control | Daw, Niv & Dayan (2005), Nature Neuroscience 8(12):1704-1711. Habitual and goal-directed control are model-free ("caching") and model-based ("tree-search") reinforcement learners in dorsolateral striatum and prefrontal cortex. Behaviour follows whichever controller's value estimate is less uncertain under approximate Bayesian versions of each. Simulations reproduce the devaluation data: over-training yields devaluation-insensitive habit, except for actions near reward or in tasks with more actions and outcomes. Both controllers serve the same ends; neither is the "irrational" one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-459.md)), supplementary methods not read. Worth reading as the founding statement of model-based versus model-free control as two brain systems, and of arbitration between them by relative uncertainty. Goal-directed (devaluation-sensitive) behaviour is a prefrontal "tree-search" controller, statistically efficient but noisy to compute. Habit is a dorsolateral-striatal "caching" controller, cheap but data-hungry and blind to revaluation. Each controls behaviour when its value estimate is the more certain, which reproduces why over-training produces habits unless the task is complex or the action near the reward. Both controllers pursue "identical rational ends": a rejection of the impulsive-limbic-versus-rational-prefrontal picture. |

Hierarchical RL groups actions into reusable "options" with their own policies, subgoals and pseudo-reward. That eases the scaling problem by cutting the number of decisions to explore and learn. Options ease the scaling problem of RL by shrinking search and learning to a few decision points. An actor-critic version maps option identifiers to dorsolateral PFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and extended prediction errors to orbitofrontal cortex. The problem it puts first is option discovery: the wrong options cause negative transfer, as in human problem solving. |

The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

| [LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012), PNAS 109(42). In Libet's spontaneous movement task, a leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, with weak constant urgency I and a threshold, fitted only to waiting times, reproduces the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96): time-locking to threshold crossings averages up the autocorrelated noise that produced them. The "neural decision to move now" is the late threshold crossing, about 150 ms before movement, so Libet's inference of an unconscious decision a half-second earlier is unfounded. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md)); worth reading as the model that reinterprets the readiness potential. A leaky stochastic accumulator with a weak constant input ("urgency"), fitted with three parameters to 14 participants' waiting times in Libet's task, reproduces the shape of the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96) because averaging epochs time-locked to threshold crossings recovers the noise that happened to carry the accumulator there. Its prediction, that fast responses to unpredictable clicks are preceded by a slow negativity, was confirmed (13 participants). On this account the "neural decision to move now" is the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement, not the onset of the readiness potential, and Libet's inference that the brain decides before awareness is "unfounded". The authors say plainly that this shows the readiness potential could reflect spontaneous fluctuation, not that it does. |

PubMed (PMID 12240693) carries the abstract only, and there is no PubMed Central record. A web search found no author-posted or institutional copy, only the later Ramírez and Cabanac abstract (2003). | [LIT-1468](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1468.md) | Deeply Felt Affect: The Emergence of Valence in Deep Active Inference | Hesp, Smith, Parr, Allen, Friston & Ramstead (2021), Neural Computation 33(2):398–446. Valence is a state of self, inferred at a hierarchically deeper level from changes in the expected precision γ of one's action model, which weights preference-driven expected free energy against a habitual prior in policy selection. The update to γ, affective charge, is positive when outcomes raise confidence in the action model and negative when they lower it. The valence level sends priors on γ back down. A simulated rat in a T-maze with context reversal infers negative and then positive valence, and adapts better than an agent without that level. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1111](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1111.md)): in full, from the publisher's CC BY PDF as deposited in Aarhus University's repository (pure.au.dk), checked against the University of Amsterdam deposit. A deep active-inference model of valence. A precision term γ sets how far the agent's preference-driven action model, rather than a habitual prior, governs policy selection. Its update, "affective charge", is positive when outcomes raise confidence in the action model and negative when they lower it. A second, slower level infers a binary valence state from affective charge and sends priors on γ back down. Simulated in a T-maze with reversal, the agent with the valence level adapts faster than one without it. "Felt" means explicitly represented, which the authors take as necessary for self-reportable experience of valence. Filed for the record's candidate that a valence regime is felt when the system models its own potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)). |
| [LIT-1488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1488.md) v2 | The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests | Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer (2024). Across 642 independent tests, forming implementation intentions was effective for cognitive, affective and behavioural outcomes (.27 ≤ d ≤ .66). Effects were larger when plans had a contingent if-then format, participants were highly motivated to reach the goal, and plans were rehearsed. A new taxonomy of the cues and responses that plans specify is developed and its categories tested. Publication bias was substantial: the pooled d = .36 falls to d = .15 under robust Bayesian meta-analysis, a small and highly heterogeneous effect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1131.md)) from the version of record deposited in the University of Konstanz repository (KOPS, in copyright, terms of use); worth reading as the largest synthesis of if-then planning (642 experimental tests to September 2019) and the one that corrects its size. The effect is reliable (BF10 = 319) but small once publication bias is modelled (d = .15, against an uncorrected .36 and 2006's .65), and highly heterogeneous. Between tests, the conditional link beats a schedule of the same behaviour, rehearsal helps, keeping a copy to revisit hurts, and plans work only when the goal is wanted. Its taxonomy finds nearly every cue and response effective, ignoring and waiting before responding among them. No mechanism is tested. |
| [LIT-1497](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1497.md) v2 | Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes | Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests: forming an implementation intention, an if-then plan saying when, where and how a goal will be pursued, had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment (d = .65). The plans helped people start goal striving, shield it from unwanted influences, disengage from failing courses of action and conserve capacity, and the postulated processes were supported: the specified opportunity became more accessible and the response more automatic. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1124](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1124.md)) from the University of Konstanz repository's scan of the published chapter (KOPS, CC BY-NC-ND 2.0), through OCR; worth reading as the first large meta-analysis of if-then planning and the fullest statement of its mechanism: a plan hands initiation of a response decided in advance to the cue it names, so nothing is deliberated in the situation, and the plan fires only while the goal behind it is active. 94 tests, d = .65 against a goal intention alone, with large effects on cue accessibility and on the immediacy, efficiency and non-conscious running of planned responses from small sets of tests. The size is not corrected for publication bias; the 2024 review of 642 tests ([LIT-1488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1488.md)) finds the bias substantial and a corrected effect near d = .15. What happens when a plan's response proves wrong is named and left untested. |
